mots.sens: This word means 'to strike' or 'plague'. It evokes the idea of a divine intervention that brings suffering or calamity. In the context of the plagues of Egypt, 'makah' emphasizes God's power manifested through judgments against opposition to His will. Theologically, it reminds us that God is sovereign and can act to free His people from oppression.

This term means 'to send' or 'to let go'. It is often used to denote liberation or allowing someone to leave a place. In this verse, it underscores God's promise that Pharaoh will eventually release the Israelites, signifying God's victory over oppression. Spiritually, it symbolizes the deliverance that God offers to His people.

This word means 'people' and refers to a community or unified group. In the context of Exodus, it designates the people of Israel, chosen by God to be His inheritance. This highlights the collective identity of the Israelites as a nation under divine protection, and their calling to be a holy people. Theologically, it reminds us that God cares for His people and acts on their behalf.

1.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the Israelites' slavery in Egypt, during the period when Moses is called to free his people from Pharaoh's oppression.
1.passage: In this chapter, God announces the final plague that will strike Egypt before Pharaoh lets the Israelites go. This moment is crucial as it marks the culmination of divine judgments against Egypt.
1.culture: In Egyptian culture, pharaohs were considered living gods, and their power was absolute. Pharaoh's refusal to free the Israelites represents a rebellion against divine authority.
1.interpretation: This verse shows God's determination to free His people and to exercise His judgment on injustice. It emphasizes that despite Pharaoh's resistance, God's plan will be fulfilled, leading to the liberation of His people.
1.commentaire: This passage reminds us that God is sovereign and acts to free those who are oppressed. It encourages us to trust in His power and His promise of deliverance, even when circumstances seem desperate. As believers, we are called to remember that God hears the cries of His people and intervenes for our good.

mots.sens: This word means 'vessel' or 'instrument'. It designates an object used to contain or transport something, often related to precious items. In the context of this verse, it evokes not only the material value of silver and gold vessels but also their use in worship and rituals, thus highlighting the importance of preparation for a divine work.

This verb means 'to ask' or 'to inquire'. It implies an action of solicitation, often in a context of need or desire. Spiritually, this can be seen as an invitation for the community to come together and help one another, illustrating the necessity of cooperation in God's plan for the liberation of Israel.

This term means 'people'. It designates a community united by a common identity, often in relation to God's covenant. In this verse, it emphasizes the collective role of the people of Israel in fulfilling God's will, reminding that each has a part to play in God's plan.

This word means 'women'. It highlights the role of women in Israelite society, often underestimated. By mentioning them specifically, the text underscores the importance of every member of the community, regardless of gender, in realizing God's promises.

2.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the Exodus, at the time when God is preparing His people to leave Egypt after years of slavery, marking a major historical turning point for Israel.
2.passage: In Exodus 11, God announces the final plague that will strike Egypt, and He gives specific instructions to the people of Israel to prepare for their imminent liberation, emphasizing the importance of obedience and faith.
2.culture: In Egyptian culture, gold and silver objects were not only symbols of wealth but also offerings often used in worship. This cultural context enriches the understanding of the request made by God, who prepares His people to leave with material goods for their new beginning.
2.interpretation: This verse illustrates God's providence that provides for the needs of His people, even in times of transition. By asking the Israelites to solicit their Egyptian neighbors, God shows that the wealth of nations can be used for His purposes, transforming what was previously a symbol of oppression into a means of blessing.
2.commentaire: This passage reminds us that God cares about the details of our lives and prepares His people for future steps. As believers, we are called to be attentive to divine instructions and to work together to fulfill God's plans. It encourages us to see opportunities for blessing even in difficult situations, reminding us that God provides for our needs through unexpected means.

mots.sens: This word means 'grace' or 'favor'. It evokes a kindness that is undeserved, a free gift of divine favor. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes how God favored the people of Israel in the eyes of the Egyptians, demonstrating God's sovereignty in fulfilling His promises. Spiritually, it reminds us that God's grace can touch even those who are not His people.

The name 'Moses' means 'drawn out of the waters', referring to his miraculous origin. Moses is the leader chosen by God to lead His people out of slavery. His status as 'very esteemed' shows how God elevated him in the perception of the Egyptians, highlighting the importance of divine leadership in critical moments. This teaches us that God can use people to accomplish His purposes, even in hostile contexts.

This term means 'people' and often refers to a group united by a common identity. In this passage, it designates the people of Israel, who are undergoing a major transition toward freedom. This underscores the idea that God has a chosen people, and that He acts on their behalf. Theologically, it reminds us of the importance of our identity in Christ as God's people.

The word 'Pharaoh' designates the king of Egypt, representing oppression and earthly authority. In the context of this verse, he symbolizes opposition to God and His people. The way Moses is respected in the eyes of Pharaoh's servants shows that even the powerful must recognize God's authority. This teaches us that, even in the face of opposition, God can establish the dignity and respect of His people.

3.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the Israelites' slavery in Egypt, around 1446 B.C., at a time when God is preparing the deliverance of His people.
3.passage: In Exodus 11, God announces the final plague that will strike Egypt, marking the beginning of Israel's liberation. This verse highlights how Moses is viewed positively despite the tension between the Egyptians and the Israelites.
3.culture: In Egyptian culture, power and status were paramount, and the favor of leaders was often seen as a sign of divine blessing. The positive perception of Moses by the Egyptian people is therefore significant.
3.interpretation: This verse illustrates how God acts in the hearts of men to prepare the deliverance of His people. The grace granted to the Israelites and the respect enjoyed by Moses testify to God's sovereignty over the nations.
3.commentaire: This passage reminds us that God is capable of touching hearts even in the most difficult situations. As believers, we must trust in God's grace that accompanies us, even when we face opposition. Like Moses, we are called to be instruments of God, and our testimony can have an impact on those around us.

mots.sens: This term means 'destroyer' or 'devastator.' It is derived from the root 'שָׁחַת' which evokes the idea of destroying or corrupting. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the imminent divine action of judgment upon Egypt, symbolizing God's power against oppression. Theologically, it reminds us that God is sovereign and intervenes in history to free His people.

This word means 'evening' or 'night.' It evokes the moment of transition between day and night, often symbolizing moments of judgment or divine revelation in the Bible. In this verse, it marks the beginning of a decisive act of God, highlighting the urgency and gravity of the situation for the Egyptians and the Israelites. Spiritually, it can symbolize the moments when God acts in darkness to bring forth light.

This term designates Egypt, a country often associated with oppression and idolatry in the Bible. The root of the word evokes the idea of 'tightening' or 'enclosing,' which underscores the condition of slavery of the Israelites. In this context, Egypt represents not only a geographical location but also a symbol of sin and oppression that God is about to judge. It reminds believers that God is capable of delivering from all forms of spiritual slavery.

4.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the Israelites' slavery in Egypt, around the 13th century B.C., a period marked by the struggle for freedom and divine intervention.
4.passage: This verse is part of the last plagues of Egypt, where God announces the death of the firstborn as the final judgment against Egypt, emphasizing God's determination to free His people.
4.culture: In Egyptian culture, night was often perceived as a time of mystery and danger, and God's judgment upon the Egyptian gods manifests here in a spectacular way.
4.interpretation: Spiritually, this verse announces a decisive divine intervention, where God passes through the darkness to bring judgment and deliverance. It reminds believers that God is present even in the darkest moments of their lives.
4.commentaire: This passage teaches us that God is sovereign and acts to free His people from oppression. As Christians, we must remember that even in difficult times, God is at work to bring deliverance. This encourages us to trust in His power and His promise of protection for those who obey Him.

mots.sens: This word means 'firstborn' and refers to the first child born of a mother. In the biblical context, the firstborn holds particular importance, often associated with divine blessing and inheritance. Spiritually, it also represents consecration to God, as in the case of the redemption of the firstborn of Israel. The death of the firstborn in Egypt underscores the severity of divine judgment and the importance of submission to God's will.

This term means 'to die' and evokes the cessation of life. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the gravity of God's judgment against Egypt for its obstinacy. Death, in the Bible, is often the result of sin and disobedience, and here it serves as a powerful symbol of separation from God. It also reminds us of the necessity of repentance and submission to God to escape judgment.

This word designates Egypt, a country often associated with oppression and idolatry in the Bible. Spiritually, Egypt represents the world and its systems opposed to God. The judgment upon Egypt, particularly the death of the firstborn, symbolizes Israel's liberation from slavery and the call to come out of sin and spiritual oppression. It underscores God's sovereignty over all nations.

5.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the Israelites' slavery in Egypt, around the 13th century B.C., during the period of God's judgments against Pharaoh and his people.
5.passage: Exodus 11 is part of the last plagues sent upon Egypt, announcing the ultimate judgment that will lead to Israel's liberation. This chapter highlights God's determination to free His people and demonstrate His power.
5.culture: In Egyptian culture, firstborns were often considered privileged, holding a high status in society. The death of the firstborn thus represents a direct assault on this hierarchy and the security of Egypt.
5.interpretation: This verse illustrates God's justice in the face of injustice and oppression. The death of the firstborn is an act of judgment, but also a call to repentance for the Egyptian people. Spiritually, it reminds us of the necessity to recognize our state before God and seek His mercy.
5.commentaire: God's judgment upon Egypt teaches us that disobedience and oppression have serious consequences. As believers, we are called to live in obedience and seek the redemption offered by Christ, our spiritual firstborn. This passage reminds us of the importance of consecration to God and the impact of our choices on our lives and the lives of others.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to cry out' or 'to shout.' It evokes an intense expression of pain or despair. In this context, it emphasizes the depth of suffering that the Egyptian people will experience due to God's judgments. Spiritually, it reminds us that the cry of the oppressed reaches heaven and that God hears the suffering of His own.

This term designates Egypt, a country symbolizing oppression and idolatry in the Bible. Egyptian, Mitzrayim is also associated with servitude, representing the forces that oppose God and His people. Theologically, this represents the struggle between God's people and the powers of evil.

This word means 'great' or 'major,' and it is often used to describe the greatness of God or significant events. In this context, it emphasizes the magnitude of the cries that will resound in Egypt, indicating an unprecedented calamity. It reminds us of God's power in His judgments and the seriousness of disobedience.

6.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the Exodus, around 1446 B.C., when God was judging Egypt for its oppression of the people of Israel.
6.passage: Exodus 11 is part of the last plagues that God sends upon Egypt before the liberation of the Israelites. This chapter announces the plague of the death of the firstborn, highlighting the severity of divine judgment.
6.culture: In Egyptian culture, cries were often associated with mourning rituals and despair. The mention of cries in this context underscores the emotional and spiritual impact of God's judgments on an idolatrous nation.
6.interpretation: This verse highlights the severity of God's judgment upon Egypt due to its obstinacy. Spiritually, it reminds us that sin has consequences and that God is just in His decisions.
6.commentaire: The cry of the Egyptians is a call to repentance and recognition of God's sovereignty. For us today, it teaches the importance of not ignoring divine warnings and seeking to live in accordance with His will. This passage also reminds us that suffering can be the result of our distance from God, and that returning to Him is always possible.

mots.sens: This word means 'destroyer' or 'devastator.' It is derived from the root 'שָׁחַת' (shāḥat), which evokes the idea of destroying or corrupting. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes God's power to distinguish between the Egyptians and the Israelites, preserving the latter group from the destruction that falls upon Egypt.

This name, often translated as 'The LORD,' is the proper name of God in the Hebrew tradition. It evokes the idea of a constant presence and a personal relationship with His people. In this verse, He is the guarantor of protection and distinction between those who belong to Him and those who are under His judgment.

This word means 'lamb' and is often associated with sacrifices in Israelite worship. It represents innocence and submission, and in the context of the Exodus, it foreshadows the sacrifice of Christ. The mention of animals here underscores the extent of divine protection that extends even to creation.

7.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the Israelites' slavery in Egypt, around the 13th century B.C., during the ten plagues that precede their liberation.
7.passage: This verse is part of God's instructions to Moses regarding the last plague, the death of the firstborn, and highlights the divine distinction between Israel and Egypt.
7.culture: In Egyptian culture, animals held great importance and were often revered. The mention of the protection of Israelite animals underscores God's power over all creatures.
7.interpretation: This verse reveals God's sovereignty and His ability to protect His people from the judgments He inflicts on the nations. It also shows the separation between God's people and those who do not recognize Him.
7.commentaire: This passage reminds us that God makes a clear distinction between those who belong to Him and those who do not. As believers, we are called to live in this divine protection, recognizing the grace that has been granted to us. This encourages us to testify to our faith and to live according to God's precepts, knowing that He watches over us.

mots.sens: This word means 'to serve' or 'to work.' It is often used to denote the service rendered to a master or to God. In this context, it emphasizes the relationship of slavery and submission of the Israelites to Egypt, but also the promise of their liberation. Spiritually, it evokes the notion of servitude to God, who calls His people to serve Him freely after their deliverance.

This term means 'to bow down' or 'to worship.' It implies an act of total submission and respect towards a higher authority. In this verse, it represents the act of acknowledging God's sovereignty and the necessity of submitting to His will. Theologically, it reminds us of the importance of authentic worship and submission to God in our spiritual lives.

This word means 'to be angry' or 'to become enraged.' It expresses a strong emotion often related to injustice or rebellion. In the context of Moses, it shows his frustration at Pharaoh's hard-heartedness and the oppression of the people of Israel. Spiritually, it reminds us that anger can be a legitimate response to injustice, but it must be channeled towards righteous actions.

8.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the Exodus, around 1446 B.C., when the Israelites are enslaved in Egypt and awaiting their divine liberation.
8.passage: In Exodus 11, God announces the last plague that will strike Egypt, leading to the liberation of the Israelites. This chapter is a turning point in the history of the Exodus, marking the culmination of God's judgments against Pharaoh and the Egyptian gods.
8.culture: Egyptian culture valued power and control, both politically and religiously. Submission to Pharaoh's authority was the norm, and rebellion against him was seen as an act of despair.
8.interpretation: This verse illustrates the tension between God's authority and Pharaoh's resistance. The prostration of Pharaoh's servants before Moses symbolizes the acknowledgment of God's power and the inevitability of His people's deliverance. It also highlights the divine plan for liberation and restoration.
8.commentaire: This passage reminds us that Moses' anger was justified in the face of oppression and Pharaoh's hard-heartedness. As believers, we are called to bow down before God, acknowledging His sovereignty and power. This encourages us to be instruments of His will, even in the face of opposition, and to act with faith and determination in our spiritual walk.

mots.sens: This word means 'miracle' or 'sign' and is often used to refer to divine acts that reveal God's power. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes God's willingness to demonstrate His sovereignty through spectacular miracles, thereby strengthening the faith of His people and the judgment on Egypt. The theological significance here is that miracles are not just manifestations of power, but also means of revealing the nature of God.

The verb 'shama' means 'to listen' or 'to hear,' but it also implies a notion of obedience. In this verse, it is used to show that Pharaoh will not pay attention to divine warnings, thus highlighting his obstinacy. Spiritually, it reminds us that listening to God's voice is essential for life and deliverance.

This term refers to Egypt, but it also has a connotation of 'pressure' or 'oppression.' In the context of the Exodus, Egypt represents the place of slavery and suffering for the people of Israel. Theologically, it symbolizes the sin and oppression that God wants to deliver His people from, thus announcing a divine liberation.

9.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the Israelites' slavery in Egypt, during the period when Moses is chosen by God to lead His people to freedom.
9.passage: In chapter 11, God announces the last plague that will strike Egypt, thus preparing the way for the final deliverance of the Israelites. This verse underscores God's determination to manifest His power despite Pharaoh's obstinacy.
9.culture: At this time, Egypt was a powerful nation, and Pharaoh was considered a living god. Pharaoh's resistance to God's miracles illustrates the challenge between divine power and human pride.
9.interpretation: This verse shows that Pharaoh's lack of listening does not contradict God's plan; rather, it serves to multiply the miracles. It teaches us that even when circumstances seem desperate, God has a plan that unfolds for His glory.
9.commentaire: This passage reminds us that God even uses the obstinacy of hearts to accomplish His purposes. As believers, we must be attentive to God's voice and open to His miracles in our lives. This encourages us to trust God, even when situations seem impossible, for He is always at work for our good and His glory.

mots.sens: The name 'Moshé' means 'drawn out of the waters.' It is derived from the Hebrew verb 'mashah,' which means 'to draw' or 'to extract.' Spiritually, Moses represents the one chosen by God to deliver His people from slavery, symbolizing deliverance and divine intercession.

The term 'ototh' translates to 'miracles' or 'signs.' It refers to extraordinary events that testify to divine intervention. In this context, these miracles are tangible proofs of God's power and authority over the false gods of Egypt, emphasizing the necessity to recognize divine sovereignty.

The word 'Par'oh' refers to the pharaoh, the ruler of Egypt. Etymologically, it means 'great house,' representing earthly power and authority. Spiritually, it embodies opposition to God and His redemptive plan, illustrating the struggle between human power and divine will.

The verb 'yashav' means 'to remain' or 'to sit.' In this context, it indicates Pharaoh's resistance to freeing the children of Israel. This reflects the hardness of the human heart in response to God's call, highlighting the need for repentance and openness to divine truth.

10.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the Israelites' slavery in Egypt, around the 13th century B.C., a period marked by pharaonic dominance and polytheistic worship.
10.passage: This verse concludes a series of miracles performed by Moses and Aaron before Pharaoh, who obstinately refuses to free the people of Israel, despite the signs of God's power.
10.culture: In Egyptian culture, magic and miracles were common, and pharaohs saw themselves as gods. Pharaoh's refusal to yield to God's miracles illustrates human pride and arrogance.
10.interpretation: Spiritually, this verse shows the struggle between God's will and human stubbornness. Despite the evidence of His power, Pharaoh chooses to resist, illustrating the reality of sin that hardens the heart.
10.commentaire: This passage reminds us that even in the face of obvious signs from God, resistance can be strong. It urges us not to harden our hearts but to be receptive to the divine call. Like Moses, we are called to be witnesses of God's power in our daily lives, sharing His message of deliverance with those around us.
